source.title: Power Lines: Scaling Laws for Weight Decay and Batch Size in LLM Pre-training
source.authors: Shane Bergsma; Nolan Dey; Gurpreet Gosal; Gavia Gray; Daria Soboleva; Joel Hestness

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports new batch-size and weight-decay results in LLM pre-training, an extension to the claim’s hyperparameter and generalization-gap subject. It does not evaluate the natural-label versus random-label generalization behavior described in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper measures held-out validation loss and scaling of weight decay and batch size during LLM pre-training. Those results bear on batch-size and explicit weight-decay conditions in V4–V6, but it does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD (V4), measure a training–test error gap or test error as dropout is added (V5–V6), or measure the other versioned phenomena. The reported comparison tuning λ versus η is retained as a result about weight decay; optimizer comparisons cited from prior work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests V5 in single-epoch LLM pre-training: at fixed model size and training-token budget, increasing batch size beyond an optimum worsens held-out cross-entropy, including after weight-decay tuning. Table 1 supplies a direct comparison. A training–test gap is not required by V5, and fixed tokens in this single-epoch setting provide a common data budget.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors conclude that optimal AdamW timescale decreases with tokens per parameter, enabling weight-decay prediction; optimal and critical batch sizes scale primarily with training-data size; and weight-decay tuning improves those estimates. Their time–compute analysis also favors smaller, overtrained models under their data-parallel training-time formulation.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains GPT2-like LLMs on SlimPajama with AdamW and µP and measures validation loss, optimal weight decay, and batch-size scaling. The claim versions focus largely on classification generalization, test error, optimizer comparisons, dropout, sharpness, and memorized examples; the study does not reproduce those methods or measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes and fitted batch-size scaling laws change with weight-decay choice; the paper also reports small-batch loss degradation and notes that a single learning-rate schedule, dataset, vocabulary, and context length were used.

fits_no_version.finding: Adjusting weight decay can slightly outperform adjusting learning rate as the training-data budget changes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-decay tuning is an effective hyperparameter-scaling strategy for AdamW LLM pre-training.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixed weight decay alters fitted optimal and critical batch-size scaling relationships.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch-size scaling-law estimates depend on whether AdamW weight decay is tuned.

record.problems: Validation loss is measured on a held-out set, but the study does not report training error or a train–test error gap. It uses one dataset, vocabulary, context length, and learning-rate schedule. The authors say their full Bcrit fitting procedure was not feasible for the 3.3B model and estimated it from two batch-size/data pairs. Small batches eventually degrade loss, and the authors identify further hyperparameter tuning as a possible explanation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were omitted. Cited prior-work optimizer, batch-size, and generalization results are not this study’s own outcomes; method-selection values and figure-only points without additional textual result descriptions were not extracted as separate rows.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label versus random-label held-out performance.
Width beyond the interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, including differences under limited or broader tuning.

Image classifiers; repeated-epoch training on a fixed dataset; interventions changing normalization; and controlled tests of alternative warmup or learning-rate-scaling recipes. Additional-token comparisons do not isolate longer training on the same data.
Dropout interventions and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples.

missing.what: Additional-data compensation at 3.3B: B=2016 trained to 23TPP reaches loss 2.1688, while B=4032 trained to 30TPP reaches 2.1695. Record both conditions. This demonstrates comparable held-out loss with a larger batch and more tokens, although it does not isolate repeated-epoch training or compare batches at fixed data.

Direct textual finding underlying R4: at 111M and target loss 3.03, larger batches perform worse because fixed weight decay lets the AdamW timescale drift from its optimum. Record the attribution separately from the fitted critical-batch-size statistic; no loss difference is supplied.
missing.locator: Appendix F.5, Weight decay affects scaling of Bcrit

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for any listed version. Held-out cross-entropy is an appropriate language-model performance measure for V5. Slight degradation at very small batches establishes an interior optimum; it does not contradict V5's workload-dependent large-batch threshold.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or natural-label held-out accuracy comparison.
No width sweep across the interpolation threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD held-out performance comparison.

No image-classification or language-model comparison of large and small batches under fixed epoch budgets; no test-error gap measurement. The study varies batch size in LLM pre-training and reports held-out validation loss, and tests tuned versus fixed weight decay.
No dropout intervention or dropout versus weight-decay removal comparison.
No sharpness or norm/margin generalization-measure comparison.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: 610M
rows.operation_detail: Swept λ at each batch size and reported the tuned validation loss at 20TPP; compared tuning λ with tuning η and default λ=0.1.
rows.baseline: Tuned η with default λ=0.1; table also lists fixed η̃=1.6e-02 and λ=0.1.
rows.note: The metric is held-out validation loss, but there is no small-batch comparison under fixed epochs or training-error measure. The table compares tuning λ with tuning η; these values do not isolate a general large-batch penalty.
rows.check: The values are correct, but the state and interpretation are wrong. All runs use the same 610M model and 12.1B training tokens at 20TPP. With tuned weight decay, validation loss rises from 2.563 at B=252 to 2.891 at B=8064. This directly measures a large-batch penalty under a common training-data budget. Split the batch conditions and tuning strategies into separate rows; the smallest batches also perform slightly worse than B=252.

source_check.correct: Tuned λ losses at B=63,126,252,504,1008,2016,4032,8064 are 2.579,2.565,2.563,2.570,2.592,2.637,2.733,2.891. All use the same 610M model and 12.1B training tokens in single-epoch pre-training. State observed is appropriate for V5.
source_check.problem: The row's note incorrectly denies a fixed-epoch small-batch comparison; the stored verdict-fix assertion that observed is wrong is also incorrect.

rows.subject: 111M
rows.operation_detail: Compared default hyperparameters, tuning η, and tuning λ as dataset size changes at B not stated.
rows.note: This is a comparison of hyperparameter tuning strategies as D changes; the text does not give the batch size or compare large and small batches at fixed epochs.
rows.check: This compares hyperparameter-tuning strategies at one model/data setting, without a batch-size contrast. It does not test V5 or the optimizer comparison in V4.

rows.subject: LLM models across scales and TPP settings
rows.operation_detail: Compared tuned and fixed weight decay in batch-size sweeps and reported resulting Bopt scaling fits and validation-loss effects.
rows.measure: Fitted Bopt power law, R², and projected Bopt values
rows.baseline: Tuned λ: Bopt = 0.0306D^0.383; R²=0.984; projected values 207, 500, 1207 at D=1e10, 1e11, 1e12.
rows.note: This reports batch-size scaling-law fits and projections, not test error or an epoch-fixed large-versus-small batch comparison.
rows.check: These are fitted locations of loss minima, fit-quality statistics, and projected hyperparameter choices. They do not record the magnitude of held-out degradation between batch conditions. Retain as contextual scaling results rather than direct claim-effect rows.

rows.subject: 111M
rows.operation_detail: Compared estimated critical batch size at target validation loss 3.03 with tuned versus fixed weight decay.
rows.locator: Appendix F.5, Weight decay affects scaling of Bcrit
rows.note: The paper says the larger-batch runs perform worse solely because τ drifts from its optimal value in this comparison. This is an estimated critical batch size, not held-out test error or an epoch-budget comparison.
rows.check: The numbers correctly describe fitted critical batch sizes, but this row measures a derived threshold rather than held-out performance at fixed training budget. The accompanying text attributes an additional large-batch penalty to untuned weight decay; that direct performance finding should be recorded separately.
